whatYouSee: The end of the left internal carotid artery is narrowed and a hazy cloud of tiny collateral vessels fills the base of the brain like a puff of smoke.
whyItMatters: Moyamoya is a progressive narrowing of the ends of the internal carotid arteries. The brain grows fragile collateral vessels to compensate and moyamoya means puff of smoke in Japanese. Children get strokes and TIAs that are often triggered by crying or hyperventilation.
treatment: Surgical revascularisation brings new blood flow to the brain. Antiplatelet drugs are used to lower the stroke risk.
takeaway: Narrowed carotid ends with a puff of smoke collateral network is moyamoya.

defects: Unexplained additional image findings: ["Dense tangled nidus-like vascular cluster in the central/right supratentorial region with serpentine vessels, which reads as an AVM rather than moyamoya collaterals","Large tortuous cervical and petrous ICA with a hairpin loop, much more prominent than expected","Separate branching vessel pattern on the image left that does not connect coherently to the injected carotid, so the injection source and laterality are unclear"]

findings: Frontal (AP) projection digital subtraction-style catheter angiogram of the head and neck, with iodinated contrast in the arterial phase.
Contrast opacifies a tortuous internal carotid artery on the image right of the neck, with a looping petrous/cavernous course, and fills the intracranial branches.
A dense, tangled cluster of small serpentine vessels lies in the central to image-right supratentorial region, consistent with a nidus.
The nidus is fed by enlarged branches arising from the supraclinoid ICA/MCA–ACA territory. No definite early draining vein is clearly shown on this single frame.
On the image left, a separate injected vessel shows an MCA/ACA-type branching pattern with a prominent sylvian-type loop and distal cortical branches. It is separate from the nidus.
Overall the cortical arterial branches appear otherwise normal in caliber, with no definite occlusion.
Skull, facial bones, dentition and shoulders are visible in the background, with no obvious fracture.
differential: Cerebral arteriovenous malformation (brain AVM) with a compact nidus
Hypervascular tumor with tumor blush, such as a vascular glioma or metastasis (less likely given the discrete tangled nidus)
Dural or pial arteriovenous fistula (less likely, since a discrete nidus is seen)
anatomyConcerns: The injected vessel pattern is unusual: the large tortuous vessel with the nidus is on the image right, while a separate branching vessel is on the image left. This could reflect crossflow through the anterior communicating artery or a bilateral/overlapping projection, and it needs confirmation of the injected vessel and laterality.
The marked cervical ICA tortuosity looping appears to be a normal variant or acquired, and is not impossible anatomy.
No definite impossible anatomy is seen; the apparent asymmetry is probably due to projection, head rotation or crossflow.

clueFacts.fact: In moyamoya disease, headaches are common and can occur because reduced blood flow and the dilated collateral vessels at the base of the brain may irritate pain-sensitive structures.

clueFacts.clue: an arm that sometimes felt heavy
clueFacts.fact: In moyamoya disease, an arm that feels heavy can reflect a TIA, since narrowed carotid ends reduce blood flow to the brain area that controls arm movement, causing temporary weakness.
